citation.title: Editorial Bias in Crowd-Sourced Political Information

standing_assumptions:
The article (PLOS ONE 10(9): e0136327, published September 2, 2015; eight pages, printed page n/8 = PDF page n) is an empirical report of randomized field experiments on Wikipedia. It has no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof, no displayed formula and no formal notation; its quantitative statements are in running text, in Fig 1 and in the tables of the twelve Supporting Information files S1–S12. The supplements are DOCX files with no fixed pagination: ‘rendered p.’ below is the page of the validators' renderings of those files, saved under the artifact folders that the targets name. Everything quoted below was read from page images: the main article from staged/pages/p-N.png, the supplements from those renderings.
(S1) Studies and populations. p. 2/8–3/8 (PDF pp. 2–3): “During the summer and fall of 2014, we conducted four studies on Wikipedia, all of which followed the same basic design. Studies 1, 2, and 4 were conducted on the English-language Wikipedia pages of the 100 current U.S. senators, while Study 3 was conducted on the 151 English-language Wikipedia pages of senators who have passed away or otherwise left the Senate since 1990 and do not currently hold any elective office or serve as a Cabinet Secretary.”
(S2) Treatments. p. 3/8 (PDF p. 3): “In each study, research assistants collected one true positive and one true negative fact from a reputable news source on each senator that was not currently mentioned on that senator’s Wikipedia page. [...] For each study, we then randomly assigned half of the pages to have a positive fact added to the page and the other half to have a negative fact added to the page.” “In Studies 1 and 4, we used a factorial design, where we also randomized half of the pages to include a citation with the fact, and the other half without a citation. In Studies 2 and 3, we always included a citation. S1–S4 Files present randomization checks and report the expected covariate balance across the treatment conditions for each study. In S5 File, we report one concluding study to replicate Studies 1 and 4 that was partially aborted due to problems in the implementation, the inclusion of which does not change the results.”
(S3) Implementation. p. 3/8 (PDF p. 3), ‘Implementation on Wikipedia’: “After the facts were collected and senators were randomly assigned to experimental conditions, we inserted the facts into the corresponding senator’s Wikipedia article in the section that seemed most appropriate. In order to prevent confounding, the order in which the edits were made, the time of day, the name of the editing Wikipedia account, and the IP address used to make the edit were randomly assigned as well. With the exception of Study 1, new accounts were created before each study began and were seeded with true, cited, political, non-Senate edits to Wikipedia. More details are presented in S1–S4 Files.” S1 File (rendered p. 1), ‘Details of Random Assignment’: “Senators were first randomly assigned into 25 blocks of 4. Within each block, 2 senators were randomly assigned to receive a negative fact and 2 were randomly assigned to receive a positive fact. Independent of the type of fact, 2 senators were randomly assigned to have the fact cited and 2 senators were randomly assigned to have the fact uncited. The date, time, and account used to make the edits were randomly assigned as well .”
(S4) Outcome and model. p. 4/8 (PDF p. 4), ‘Estimation of Experimental Effects’: “Our primary dependent variable is the survival time of the facts–the amount of time between when the fact is added to Wikipedia and when it is removed. To assess the statistical difference in the survival times between the experimental conditions, we use a Cox proportional hazard model [32].” p. 4/8, Results: “Pooling across studies, negative facts are far more likely to be removed than positive facts by other Wikipedia editors (hazard ratio = 1.59, a measure of the rate at which an event happens in one treatment group over another, p = 0.001).”
(S5) Conventions of the supplementary tables. In the Cox tables of the supplements each entry stands under ‘Coefficient:’ with a parenthesized entry under ‘Standard error:’ beneath it (S6, S9 and S10 were read for this list; finding P041-N013 records the same heading in S7 and S8), and the tables of S6, S9 and S11 used below each carry a note of the form “*Significant at the 10% level; **Significant at the 5% level; ***Significant at the 1% level; Fixed Effects refer to fixed effects for study wave; Covariates Yes means controlling for the date and time order in which an edit was randomly assigned to be made, a binary variable for Republicans, Senate class, region (NE, S, W), length of incumbency, log of Wikipedia page character count before Study 1 began, log of state population, and a dichotomous influence variable for party leaders and committee chairs.” (S10's note stops after “Fixed Effects refer to fixed effects for study wave”. The note of S6 Table E has in addition, after the legend of the stars, “^Date of entry, and hour of entry removed to avoid convergence issues;”, the caret being attached to ‘Yes^’ in the Covariates row of the column ‘5 (1st Half)’.) The entries headed ‘Coefficient:’ in the Cox tables are hazard ratios (exponentiated Cox coefficients) for positive against negative facts and for cited against uncited facts, with standard errors on the hazard-ratio scale: S6 Table A (‘Pooled Cox Regression Estimates’, rendered p. 1) prints Positive 0.629*** (0.091), N 300, and Cited 0.429*** (0.069), N 200, and the main text's 1.59 and 2.33 are their reciprocals (finding P041-N013, rated a clarity note). The paper does not say how the stars are computed.
(S6) Not in the paper: the deposited data. The replication archive (Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/WT4I9N, V1.0; staged/code/harvard-dataverse-WT4I9N-v1.0/) has 551 rows: 100 for each of Studies 1, 2, 4 and 5 and 151 for Study 3. Its codebook codes treatment 1 as positive and cited, 2 as positive and uncited, 3 as negative and cited, 4 as negative and uncited. Studies 1, 2 and 4 each have 50 positive and 50 negative facts; Studies 1 and 4 each have 50 cited and 50 uncited facts; Study 3 has 75 positive and 76 negative facts. Following the deposited do-file (lines 11–15), a fact counts as removed by a horizon of $h$ hours when it has a recorded removal and its stored duration in milliseconds, multiplied by $2.77778\times10^{-7}$, is at most $h$; a fact with no recorded removal survives every horizon used here. The counts used in the targets (removals by 4, 6, 12, 24, 72 and 168 hours, by study and arm) were recounted from the staged CSV when this list was fixed and agree with the validators' artifacts.
(S7) Rounding. A number printed with three decimals as $v$ stands for a value in $[v - 0.0005,\ v + 0.0005]$; a whole-number percentage $k$ is the rounding of $x$ when $k - \tfrac12 \le x < k + \tfrac12$. No quantity used below lies at a rounding tie.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: ‘Replication on Wikipedia Pages of Dead and Retired Senators’ (the whole paragraph), with the last sentence of the first paragraph of the Discussion and the last two sentences of the Abstract; as printed
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. ‘Replication on Wikipedia Pages of Dead and Retired Senators’ (p. 5/8): “Wikipedia has special guidelines for articles that are biographies of living persons that require a more conservative approach to avoid libel [34]. To ensure that this more conservative approach does not explain our finding of editorial bias, Study 3 conducted a replication on the Wikipedia pages of senators who have left office since 1990. Both among senators who have left office and are still living and those who have passed away, we find no differences in the rates in which positive and negative facts are removed ($p$ = 0.70 and 0.47, respectively and $p$ = 0.42, pooled). If anything, the positive facts were removed more quickly than the negative ones. This suggests that the editorial bias cannot be explained by Wikipedia’s culture in general or by policies concerning biographies of living persons in particular. Instead, our findings suggest the editorial bias is limited to active politicians, the types of people for whom the stakes of a positive public image are the highest.”
Discussion, first paragraph (p. 5/8): “This experiment demonstrated that a substantial editorial bias exists for the Wikipedia pages of current U.S. senators. Across four studies, we consistently find that negative facts are more likely to be removed and are removed more quickly than positive facts. In a test conducted on the Wikipedia pages of recently retired and deceased senators, we find no editorial bias, suggesting that this bias is limited to the pages of active politicians and is not systemic to Wikipedia.”
Abstract (p. 1/8): “We replicate this study on the Wikipedia pages of deceased as well as recently retired but living senators and find no evidence of an editorial bias in either. Our results demonstrate that crowd-sourced information is subject to an editorial bias that favors the politically active.”
Qualification the paper attaches (Discussion, second paragraph, p. 5/8): “The reasons for the editorial bias toward positivity are not necessarily nefarious. It is plausible that Wikipedia editors are simply more conservative in applying their guidelines for living persons to active U.S. Senators than recently retired U.S. senators, even if the editing policies are nominally identical for both types of articles.”
Formalizable content of the passage, in the notation of P041-T2 and P041-T8 ($z(h,s) = h\log(h)/s$, $p = 2\,\Phi(-|z|)$). (P1) [The three p values] The printed pairs of S6 Table C, $(0.691,\ 0.318)$ pooled, $(0.775,\ 0.503)$ living and $(0.627,\ 0.406)$ deceased, give $|z| = 0.8032$, $0.3927$ and $0.7209$ and $p = 0.4219$, $0.6945$ and $0.4710$; over the rounding intervals of the printed pairs $p$ lies in $[0.4205,\ 0.4232]$, $[0.6936,\ 0.6954]$ and $[0.4700,\ 0.4720]$. These agree with the printed 0.42 (pooled), 0.70 (living) and 0.47 (deceased) to the precision the table entries allow, and in each case $|z| < 1$: none of the three comparisons is significant. This part of the passage is correct. (P2) [The inference] ‘we find no differences … This suggests that the editorial bias cannot be explained by … Instead, our findings suggest the editorial bias is limited to active politicians’ and ‘we find no editorial bias, suggesting that this bias is limited to the pages of active politicians and is not systemic to Wikipedia’ are read, for the purpose of the counterexample, as the implication: if the positive-against-negative comparison is statistically clear on active senators' pages and is not detected on former senators' pages, where the absolute contrast is also smaller, then the relative bias is absent on former senators' pages. P041-T1 refutes this implication, and P041-T2 (a) to (c) show that the printed estimates do not distinguish the hazard ratio on former senators' pages either from 1 or from the hazard ratio on active senators' pages.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. ‘Editorial bias’ (p. 2/8): “Editorial bias refers to the idea that certain types of information are more likely to be removed from Wikipedia, resulting in a potentially incomplete article.” The populations and treatments: standing assumptions (S1), (S2); the outcome and the Cox model: (S4). The result for active senators (p. 4/8): “Pooling across studies, negative facts are far more likely to be removed than positive facts by other Wikipedia editors (hazard ratio = 1.59, a measure of the rate at which an event happens in one treatment group over another, $p$ = 0.001).” S6 Table A and S6 Table C: quoted in P041-T1. The paper defines neither ‘limited to’ nor ‘systemic’ and states no test of a difference between the two populations.
Not in the paper: the rendering (P2) of the inference, which follows Sol's natural reading (‘“cannot be explained” and “limited ... and is not systemic” extend nondetection and early absolute contrasts to an exclusion/restriction that these analyses do not establish’); the calculation of a p value from a printed pair, as in P041-T2.
canonical_claim.note: Not a mathematical statement of the paper: an empirical comparison and an interpretation drawn from it, listed because P041-E006 is rated Major and the brief asks for the statement as printed. Read from the page image of p. 5/8 and p. 1/8; the transcription agrees with the validator's (derivation.md, section 1). (P1) holds; the living-senator value computed from the rounded table entries is 0.694–0.695 against the printed 0.70, a difference within what the rounding of the entries allows (the reproduction recovers all three printed p values from the data). (P2) is this audit's rendering for the purpose of the counterexample, not the paper's wording; it is expected to be recorded as refuted through P041-T1, with P041-T2 as the replacement. Lean cannot decide whether the bias is in fact confined to active politicians, and the validators do not claim that it is not (‘No proof that substantive confinement to active politicians is empirically false’). If nothing can be stated beyond the implication that P041-T1 already refutes, not_applicable is the right status for (P2). The sentence ‘If anything, the positive facts were removed more quickly than the negative ones’ is the separate candidate P041-N009, which was not confirmed. The abstract's ‘find no evidence’ and the claim that the bias favors the politically active are not in question.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, the sentence giving ‘36%’ and ‘29%’, and ‘Effects of Citations on Survival’, the sentence giving ‘64%’; as printed (headline claims P041-H2 and P041-H3)
canonical_claim.location: Abstract, p. 1/8 (PDF p. 1); ‘Effects of Citations on Survival’, sentence running from p. 4/8 to p. 5/8 (PDF pp. 4–5)
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. Abstract (p. 1/8): “By randomly assigning factually true but either positive or negative and cited or uncited information to the Wikipedia pages of U.S. senators, we uncover substantial evidence of an editorial bias toward positivity on Wikipedia: Negative facts are 36% more likely to be removed by Wikipedia editors than positive facts within 12 hours and 29% more likely within 3 days. Although citations substantially increase an edit’s survival time, the editorial bias toward positivity is not eliminated by inclusion of a citation.”
‘Effects of Citations on Survival’ (pp. 4/8–5/8): “Overall, we find large and statistically significant differences in the survival time of cited and uncited facts. Consistent with Wikipedia’s policy, uncited (but true) facts are 64% more likely to be removed than cited facts within four hours (hazard ratio = 2.33, $p<0.001$).”
Formalizable content, with $R$, $M$ and the rounding rule of P041-T3 and the counts 75 and 52 of 150 (12 hours), 92 and 69 of 150 (72 hours), 62 and 32 of 100 (4 hours). (P1) [The printed numbers under the formula that produced them] $M(75,52) = 4600/127$, $M(92,69) = 200/7$ and $M(62,32) = 3000/47$ round to 36, 29 and 64. This is correct arithmetic. (P2) [The printed numbers under the printed wording] ‘36% more likely … than positive facts’, ‘29% more likely’ and ‘64% more likely … than cited facts’ are read as $R(75/150, 52/150) \in [35.5, 36.5)$, $R(92/150, 69/150) \in [28.5, 29.5)$ and $R(62/100, 32/100) \in [63.5, 64.5)$. All three are false: the values are $575/13$, $100/3$ and $375/4$ (P041-T3). (P3) [The direction] In each comparison the first group has the larger proportion removed: $75/150 > 52/150$, $92/150 > 69/150$ and $62/100 > 32/100$. This is correct.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper: the populations, treatments and outcome, standing assumptions (S1), (S2), (S4); the comparisons are negative against positive facts on the pages of sitting senators (Studies 1, 2, 4) and uncited against cited facts in Studies 1 and 4 (p. 4/8: “in Studies 1 and 4 we randomly assigned positive and negative facts to either include a citation or to have no citation”). The paper prints neither the removal counts nor a formula for the percentages. The hazard ratio 2.33 in the second sentence is the reciprocal of the 0.429 of S6 Table A and is not in question.
From the deposited data and code: the counts and the expression that produced the printed numbers, as in P041-T3.
canonical_claim.note: Not a theorem of the paper: three empirical percentages, listed because P041-E001 is rated Moderate and the brief asks for the statement as printed. Read from the page images of pp. 1, 4 and 5. The second sentence is also headline claim P041-H3 and the passage of P041-N006. (P1) and (P3) hold; (P2), the reading that the wording carries, is false and is expected to be recorded as refuted through P041-T3, with P041-T4 as the replacement. The reading in (P2) is Sol's (‘The article gives no convention redefining this directional wording as a symmetric percentage difference’).
